planting.note: Direct sow or plant plugs in spring into lean, cool, moisture-retentive mountain soil in full sun; mountain oatgrass is the dominant sod-forming bunchgrass of the southern Appalachian grassy balds and establishes best at elevation where summers stay cool and humid.

directions: Plant plugs or divisions in spring into lean, well-drained, acidic mountain soil in full sun to very light shade; mountain oatgrass forms dense, upright tufts of flattened culms and is the principal matrix grass of the open, treeless grassy balds of the Roan Highlands, Grandfather Mountain, and the Black Mountains above roughly 5,000 feet. It differs from the related poverty oatgrass (Danthonia spicata) in its taller, more erect growth and preference for consistently moist, cool, high-elevation sites rather than dry lowland ground, and is used by conservation groups to restore and maintain bald openings against woody encroachment. Mow or hand-cut annually in late fall to suppress shrub seedlings if using it to mimic bald management, and avoid rich, fertilized garden soil, which causes lax, floppy growth. It is an important host and seed source for native bald-associated insects and grassland sparrows where balds are large enough to support them.
sources: Weakley's Flora of the Southeastern United States

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into thin, gritty, acidic mountain soil in full sun to partial shade; this dwarf shrub naturally roots into rock crevices and shallow humus pockets on exposed balds and outcrops.

directions: Plant in thin, gritty, humus-poor, acidic soil in full sun to light shade, mimicking the exposed granite domes, heath balds, and grassy bald margins of the southern Blue Ridge where it naturally grows above roughly 3,000 feet. Blue Ridge St. John's wort is a low, mat-forming, semi-woody dwarf shrub with small opposite leaves and bright golden-yellow, five-petaled flowers held just above the foliage in mid-to-late summer, spreading slowly by creeping stems that root where they touch moist rock crevices. It tolerates poor, droughty, thin soils far better than rich garden beds and is best used in a native rock garden, scree, or crevice planting rather than conventional borders. Give it excellent drainage and avoid competition from taller perennials, which will quickly shade it out.
sources: Weakley's Flora of the Southeastern United States

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions or seedlings in spring into average to moist, well-drained soil in a sunny clearing or partial-shade woodland edge; Fraser's loosestrife naturally colonizes bald margins, high-elevation road banks, and forest openings in the southern Blue Ridge.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in a sunny opening or lightly shaded woodland edge, the same conditions it occupies naturally along grassy bald margins, roadbanks, and forest clearings at mid-to-high elevations in the Blue Ridge of North Carolina, Tennessee, Georgia, and Alabama. Fraser's loosestrife is an erect perennial with whorls of three to four lance-shaped leaves per node and upright spikes of golden-yellow flowers marked with a reddish-orange basal blotch in early-to-mid summer, taller and more clearing-adapted than the common wetland loosestrifes. It is globally uncommon and state-tracked in several states, so source only nursery-propagated stock from reputable Southern Appalachian native specialists rather than wild-collected material. Deadhead or leave seed heads for winter interest, and divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous bloom.
sources: Weakley's Flora of the Southeastern United States
